title: How am I supposed to put my sprites in my game?? [XP]

posts.author: Globbo
posts.body:
Ok, so the title is a bit misleading. I
do
know how to put my sprites on a template and upload them, but- that just takes so long??? like. I have a bunch of 16x16 sprites i made saved on my computer id like to use, both for my characters AND tilesets.
The tilesets are fine I guess, I can just copy and paste the sprite, and slowly align it with a template i find online, and then get rid of any excess template grids before I import it to RPG maker, but the main issue I have is with character sprites.
The templates help a bit, but they don't really help at all with the height and width? like. If i copy and paste all my sprites to a character template, I essentially have to import it, set the texture to a character, run a playtest, and then walk all around to make sure the sprite is aligned (which, you know, it never is.), go back to my editing program (GIMP), and have to take meticulous detail in aligning each sprite juuuust right so that it doesnt bounce around (for example, my left facing sprite is 2 or 3 pixels above where the center sprite is aligned at.), which usually takes at least 4 to 5 more rounds of me exporting from gimp, importing to rpg maker, making sure the sprite is set on the character, and then play testing it to make sure every sprite is aligned. It is infuriating and genuinely 7/8ths of my RPG maker playtime on steam is just me in my editing program making sure everything is aligned or putting my sprites in templates so rpg maker can read it rather than actually working on my game.
This is a problem I struggle with a
lot
and i just. never see anyone else talk about this?? is there some secret way everyone takes their sprites, and uses some program that takes these images and puts them into a sprite sheet? Is it just a skill issue on my part? is this just something everyone has to go through when adding custom sprites?

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
I'm confused by the portions that you say are giving you such difficulty.
GIMP allows you to turn on grid lines in any dimensions you want - there's no need to use a visible template that you delete later.
It also shows you at all times on the bottom the coordinates of your mouse cursor. Similarly, any time you're moving a selected portion of an image, it shows the coordinates and how far you've moved it.
You can
also
zoom in more than close enough to see the individual pixels.
I just don't get why you would have to go into the game to see whether your images are aligned or not.

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
Globbo said:
So, I should state, I am not a digital artist by any means
Click to expand...
I don't say this to make you feel bad or anything, but just as a point of reference - I am also not a digital artist by any definition of the word. What I know about image editors I've learned from using the included help file documentation and by Googling terms.
Globbo said:
how did you turn on the grid?
Click to expand...
You set what size the grid is under Image -> Configure Grid. You turn it on under View -> Show Grid, and you can also turn on View -> Snap to Grid.
Globbo said:
as far as the pixel count at the bottom goes, how is that supposed to help me?
Click to expand...
You do math. To use random numbers as an example, if you know your cels are 48 pixels across and the left-side leg edge (or strand of hair, or shoulder, or something else that's not moving on the sprite) is 3 pixels from the edge, that means you make sure that leg edge is at X coordinate 3, then 51, then 99, etc.
Globbo said:
I am also unsure how zooming in would help any frankly
Click to expand...
Because it helps you to see something like a one-pixel error. In the screenshot I showed above demonstrating zooming in, you can clearly that both sprites have their left legs against the bottom pixel of their cel - you could just as clearly see if one of them didn't.
Globbo said:
To me, this looks fine. my sprites are on the tilesheet, and im ready to export, and import into RPG maker.
Click to expand...
Everyone's eyes and brain are going to be a bit different, and I suppose experience probably helps some...but, again, no offense, but I can pretty clearly see that's really far from aligned horizontally. It's absolutely going to bounce up and down.
Look how very different amounts of hair are going up past this straight line.
This is exactly where looking at the coordinates could help you - if that actor's head is supposed to be staying level, then you would find the top-most pixel and make sure it's at the same Y coordinate going across the row.
Globbo said:
Are you just magic? do you just know instantly where a sprite needs to be positioned before you save your sprite sheets??
Click to expand...
No, and yes, in order
Again, it's just math. You know from RPG Maker's instructions how to calculate the size of your cels, you know from drawing it how large your sprites are, so where to position them on the sheet is just division and addition.

Just as a general comment: have you watched any pixel art tutorials? If you're going to use GIMP you should watch tutorials, as the abundance of options can be very daunting. Personally I use Aseprite for spriting, and GIMP for more "complex" operations like scaling and masking (two things Aseprite cannot do properly). Each tool has its own strength and weaknesses.
But if you MUST use GIMP, and if for some reason you feel you need a template for the gridlines (which is totally fine, I've seen pixel artists on YouTube work this way too), you can just add a bottom layer with the grid drawn on it. Just hide the bottom layer when you export the sprite sheet and it won't be there in your export.

I will try to address your questions, but at a certain point one can't say anything in a different way than how you've seen it before; and if it just doesn't make sense to you for some reason, then I guess it doesn't.
I will also say that I think this is a hard thing for someone with a math disability to do. You may be spending more time doing this than it's worth to just start with sprites that are formatted for RPG Maker.
Globbo said:
So, I am not very math inclined, and I've been told I have a learning disability with math, but. This still doesnt make any sense? The only numbers I can find, and that have any significance to my brain is the size of the sprites themselves, and the total canvas size, and I'm still not entirely sure what math I am supposed to do with these to get it to fit.
Click to expand...
You appear to be approaching this from kind of the opposite direction.
The first thing you should know is the dimensions of your actor image. That's the tallest and the widest in any of its frames. If that's asymmetrical, you account for that on both sides.
A good example is the dude above in the pose where the bandanna is flopping out - I'd take that in both directions and see how wide it is.
So the X dimension of a cel is 113 pixels (I'm going off of the screenshot you posted, which is probably not the actual size of the image.
You do the same thing, find the tallest pose and that's the Y dimension. I'm just gonna go with the same example frames and say it's 158.
Once you know what the dimension of
one cel
must be,
then
you determine the canvas size by multiplying each direction by 4. So your spritesheet would be 452x632. Then you set your grid to the size for one cel, 113x158.
Then you just make sure, as I explained above, that a common reference point - such as the top of the head - is in the same place in each cel.

i supposed to put the sprite then? I mean, should I just align the top of the hair with the border of the canvas?
Click to expand...
Whatever frame(s) have the feet going furthest down should be touching the bottom of the cel, as I showed you in post #2.
Globbo said:
And how do I figure out the same thing for horizontal alignment?
Click to expand...
You take whatever you found to be your widest frames and make the left/right (whichever is extended) side touch that side of the cel.
